teaching_blocks.title: Define the Prediction Task
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine an operations team wants an estimate before deciding which delivery orders need attention. ‘Predict a late delivery’ sounds clear until two engineers use different decision times or different meanings of late. A task record makes those choices explicit before you prepare examples.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Define the prediction problem in terms of the inference to be generated and the example data needed to support it. Inputs for a prediction must be information available at its prediction time, not information that only becomes available afterward. An empirical outcome proportion is the count of that outcome divided by the total count in the specified population; a conditional outcome proportion uses only the count in its specified conditioning group.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Write the task record with one prediction unit, a target event or value, the time a prediction is made and the horizon over which the target is judged, so the example/target relationship is unambiguous.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this invented task, one prediction unit is an order at acceptance. The target event is arrival more than 30 minutes after acceptance, judged over that 30-minute horizon. Distance and the promised delivery zone are available at acceptance; the eventual arrival time is not an input. Suppose a supplied population contains 100 orders, of which 20 meet the target event. Its empirical outcome proportion is 20/100 = 0.20. Within a specified zone, 12 of 40 orders meet it, giving a conditional proportion of 12/40 = 0.30. The denominators answer different questions: all orders versus orders in that zone. Record both the population and the horizon beside the counts so another engineer can interpret the same task.

Notice how changing the prediction unit would change the task. If the unit were a whole delivery zone rather than an individual accepted order, neither the input row nor the target event in this fixture would be the same. Similarly, a horizon of one hour would ask a different question from the stated 30 minutes. Keep unit, decision time, target and horizon in separate record fields so those changes cannot masquerade as implementation details. When reporting 0.30 for the zone, say which zone and which eligible orders provided the denominator. The task definition establishes the interpretation that subsequent dataset and model work must preserve.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A target is not interchangeable with an input. The later arrival can establish whether this example met the target, but cannot become information supplied to a prediction made at acceptance. Nor does the zone proportion describe every zone.

video_need.reason: A timeline and a small count table help connect decision time, target horizon and the two conditioning populations.

coverage.learning_objective: Accept or reject a numerical input against a declared rank and batch/feature-axis contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Numerical Arrays for ML
teaching_blocks.content: Your prediction fixture declares two features per order. Before doing any arithmetic, you need to distinguish three observations with two features from one flat collection of six values. Array rank and axis lengths make that distinction inspectable.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Create an array from the supplied list or tuple fixture with import numpy as np and np.array(fixture); inspect its ndim, shape and dtype. For a declared two-axis batch/feature contract, check a.ndim == 2 and compare a.shape[1] to the declared feature count before accepting the input. The shape tuple gives the length of each axis, so the batch-length requirement can be checked with a.shape[0] after checking rank.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Reject a violated input requirement with a conditional raise ValueError(message), rather than continuing with an invalid array. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Consider the fixture [[2, 10], [4, 20], [6, 30]]. The declared interpretation is three orders and two features per order, so rank 2, shape (3, 2), and feature width 2 satisfy the contract. A fixture [2, 10, 4, 20, 6, 30] contains the same number of values but has rank 1, so it fails this contract. Check rank before looking for a second axis. A rank-2 fixture with shape (3, 1) fails the feature-width rule instead. Include an accepted fixture, a declared batch-length boundary and a rejected fixture in the checks. When a production input violates the rule, raise the declared ValueError instead of allowing the later operation to decide what the input meant.

Read the shape from left to right under the declared interpretation: the first length counts observations, and the second counts features within each observation. This tells you where to check batch boundaries and where to check model input width. Do not index shape[1] before establishing rank 2; a flat failure fixture does not have that second axis. Dtype is another independent contract field. An array can have the accepted shape while using the wrong numerical representation, or the accepted dtype while having the wrong axes. Keep those failures distinguishable in tests so fixing one check does not accidentally waive another.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Total element count does not establish the meaning of the axes. Also, an assert is a fixture check during ordinary non-optimized execution, not an unconditional substitute for explicit input rejection.

context.concept_name: Choose numerical dtypes against precision and memory requirements

coverage.learning_objective: Choose a numerical representation by checking its value preservation and element-memory cost.

required_facts.statement: A numerical dtype specifies a representable value range and a bit width, so candidate integer and floating types need not preserve the same input values.
source_refs: numpy_user_guide#user/basics.types.html — Array types and conversions between types; Numerical Data Types; Overflow errors

required_facts.statement: Inspect a.dtype and explicitly cast with a.astype(candidate_dtype) when comparing representations.
source_refs: numpy_user_guide#user/basics.types.html — Array types and conversions between types; Numerical Data Types; Overflow errors

required_facts.statement: For a fixed-width numerical array, a.size × a.itemsize is its element-storage byte count, exposed by a.nbytes; it excludes non-element object overhead.
Compare the cast values with the reference values using arithmetic differences before accepting a lower-precision representation; casting can overflow or lose precision.
source_refs: numpy_user_guide#user/basics.types.html — Array types and conversions between types; Numerical Data Types; Overflow errors

teaching_blocks.title: Numerical Arrays for ML
teaching_blocks.content: An order feature matrix must fit a numerical storage budget, but a smaller representation is useful only if it preserves values well enough for the declared task. Inspect both the values and the bytes rather than selecting a dtype from its name alone.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A numerical dtype specifies a representable value range and a bit width, so candidate integer and floating types need not preserve the same input values. Inspect a.dtype and explicitly cast with a.astype(candidate_dtype) when comparing representations. For a fixed-width numerical array, a.size × a.itemsize is its element-storage byte count, exposed by a.nbytes; it excludes non-element object overhead.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the cast values with the reference values using arithmetic differences before accepting a lower-precision representation; casting can overflow or lose precision.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a reference fixture contains six values and you are comparing fixed-width representations with element widths of eight and four bytes. Their element-storage totals are 6 × 8 = 48 bytes and 6 × 4 = 24 bytes. That comparison says nothing about other object overhead. Explicitly cast the reference into the candidate representation, inspect the candidate dtype and subtract reference values to reveal changes. For instance, if a supplied candidate represents a reference value 1.25 as 1.0, the difference is −0.25. Whether that is acceptable depends on the fixture's declared tolerance; the byte saving does not decide it. Keep the reference values available while checking the candidate, so the comparison is not between two copies of the already altered values.

Inspect a value near a declared precision or range boundary as well as ordinary values. The purpose is to expose the candidate conversion's actual difference from the retained reference, not to assume that every smaller dtype behaves badly or that every successful cast is acceptable. Compare the difference using the fixture's explicit tolerance. A zero difference on one ordinary value is not enough to waive the remaining declared fixtures. Also keep the number of elements unchanged when comparing element bytes; otherwise a reduced total could come from fewer observations instead of a narrower representation. The choice balances measured preservation with the specified storage budget.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Fewer bytes is not the same as a faithful representation. A cast can lose precision or overflow, and array.nbytes is element storage rather than the whole memory cost of using the array.

context.concept_name: Apply vectorized array operations with compatible broadcasting

coverage.learning_objective: Implement shape-correct array arithmetic and verify agreement with a bounded reference.

required_facts.statement: NumPy arithmetic operations can operate elementwise on arrays instead of executing a Python operation once per observation.
Broadcasting compares axes from the right; aligned lengths must be equal or one must be 1, and missing leading axes are treated as length 1.
Check the resulting shape as well as operand compatibility, because compatible broadcasting can expand the result to a larger shape.
Use np.testing.assert_allclose(array_result, reference_result, rtol=..., atol=...) to test agreement with the list-comprehension reference under explicit tolerances.

teaching_blocks.title: Numerical Arrays for ML
teaching_blocks.content: You want to subtract one reference value for each of two order features across three observations. Array arithmetic can express that operation without a Python operation written separately for every observation, but the axes still determine what gets combined.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: NumPy arithmetic operations can operate elementwise on arrays instead of executing a Python operation once per observation. Broadcasting compares axes from the right; aligned lengths must be equal or one must be 1, and missing leading axes are treated as length 1. Check the resulting shape as well as operand compatibility, because compatible broadcasting can expand the result to a larger shape.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Use np.testing.assert_allclose(array_result, reference_result, rtol=..., atol=...) to test agreement with the list-comprehension reference under explicit tolerances.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For the invented matrix [[2, 10], [4, 20], [6, 30]], subtract [1, 5]. The trailing feature lengths match, so the result is [[1, 5], [3, 15], [5, 25]], with shape (3, 2). Verify it against a list-comprehension reference using explicit tolerances. Now compare operands shaped (3, 1) and (1, 2): compatible broadcasting yields a (3, 2) result, not a (3, 1) result. If the contract expected one output per observation without an extra feature axis, compatibility alone would not make that result acceptable. Write the intended result shape beside the numerical reference, and check both instead of accepting an operation simply because it completed.

Work through one output row to check meaning as well as compatibility. The first row [2, 10] minus the two feature references [1, 5] becomes [1, 5]. The same reference is then applied to each later observation. A reference operation should express that intended per-feature rule, not simply duplicate an accidental broadcast. For the (3, 1) and (1, 2) case, expanding three row positions against two column positions creates six outputs. That is why validating the output shape matters even when no exception was raised. The check ties the succinct operation to a concrete result rather than treating compact syntax as correctness.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Broadcasting is not permission to combine arbitrary axes. Right-aligned compatibility and the resulting shape are separate checks; a compatible operation can still produce a larger result than intended.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Vectorization operates over axes; broadcasting aligns compatible dimensions.

teaching_blocks.content:

Suppose the target population has 60 zone-A orders and 40 zone-B orders, while the sample includes 30 A and 10 B. Target proportions are 0.60 and 0.40; sample proportions are 0.75 and 0.25. With known membership, estimated inclusion probabilities are 30/60 = 0.50 for A and 10/40 = 0.25 for B. These calculations show a supported coverage difference and unequal inclusion. They do not establish that every characteristic of either zone differs. You can also summarize a selected numerical feature with its mean and standard deviation, retaining the specified observations and divisor. If a category has no target members in the supplied denominator, do not manufacture an inclusion rate for it.

Read the ratios as separate conditional questions. The sample's 0.75 zone-A share asks which zone an included observation belongs to. The 0.50 zone-A inclusion probability asks whether a target-population zone-A observation was included. Neither is the target's 0.60 zone-A share. Naming the numerator and denominator in the record prevents a later user from interpreting a selection statistic as population prevalence. The numerical summaries are descriptive evidence for the selected values only. The supported limitation is unequal observed coverage under these supplied counts, not a claim that a particular model must fail or that an unobserved cause of selection has been established.

segments.summary: Selection bias arises when observed information does not represent the population being studied. The narrated aircraft example describes returning planes with many bullet holes in their bodies and wings but fewer near their engines. Looking only at those planes suggested adding armor where holes were most common. Wald instead argued for protecting areas with few observed holes: aircraft hit in the engine were not returning. The observed damage therefore reflected which aircraft survived to be counted, not the damage across all aircraft. Missing observations changed how the sample should be interpreted.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Let observations have IDs A and B, while the label file lists B then A. A keyed lookup attaches each label to its own observation despite the reversed order. Before constructing the label dictionary, check repeated IDs: two labels for A would otherwise compete for the same dictionary key. Compare observation and label ID sets to reveal a missing label or a label without an observation. Then inspect the matched timestamps under the supplied acceptance predicates. A label's later availability does not turn it into an input available at the earlier prediction time. Exercise reordered, duplicate, missing and declared boundary fixtures so correct row counts do not conceal incorrect correspondence.

Construct the observation-ID and label-ID sets before declaring the join complete. Their differences identify the two unmatched directions: observations without labels and labels without observations. Duplicate IDs need handling before a dictionary silently replaces a value, because set equality alone would not reveal two label rows with the same ID. After the keyed join, inspect the supplied timestamp boundary on the matched record. Key correspondence and time suitability are independent requirements: a correctly keyed label can still be unsuitable under a stated time predicate. This order of checks produces aligned, permitted examples rather than an apparently complete table whose targets belong to another row.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:

Report the target proportion within each partition: if validation contains four target events among ten examples, its proportion is 0.40. The set-intersection assertion asks whether the same group identity appears on both sides, not whether two individual order IDs repeat. Distinct observations from G1 can still violate a group boundary. In the time fixture, compare timestamp extrema or the supplied inequalities under the stated cutoff; distinct group sets do not establish temporal ordering. Reporting each partition's target prevalence helps describe what the evaluation cohort actually contains, but it does not choose the boundary retrospectively. Fix the deployment-matched interpretation first, assign observations accordingly and then inspect whether the resulting partitions satisfy it. The missing validation row is an application case for the stored statistic. It is not an extra observation from which to relearn the statistic, and the observed value 100 belongs to the held-out cohort rather than the training reference. The chosen strategy defines how the replacement is learned or supplied; the train-versus-transform boundary defines when its state may change. Preserve both choices in the bounded workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose training contains north and south. Inspect categories_ and store the category dictionary with the feature name, using the fitted order rather than inventing a new one. Under a two-column north/south mapping, a known north row has its corresponding indicator set. An unseen east row is rejected by the default error policy; with handle_unknown set to ignore, it has all-zero indicators for that feature. Keep known, unseen and missing fixtures aligned with the stored mapping. Missing values present during fit can become a learned category; missing values absent from the learned set follow the unknown-category behavior. That distinction means two missing-value fixtures may need different expectations depending on what the fit actually saw.

The output width depends on the fitted category set, not on the number of categories occurring in a particular validation batch. Keep columns aligned to the stored training mapping even if a batch contains only north. An unseen east fixture tests the explicit policy without silently extending categories_ during transformation. For the missing fixture, first ask whether missing was represented in the fit data. If yes, its learned indicator follows that mapping; if not, it follows the unknown-category rule. These checks distinguish stable column identity from changing observed batch contents. The metadata dictionary records that identity so the representation remains interpretable to downstream callers.

teaching_blocks.title: Fit and Compose Preprocessing
teaching_blocks.content: Your order dataset needs one operation for numerical columns and another for zones before the estimator receives inputs. A fitted pipeline keeps those declared transformations attached to the prediction path instead of asking each caller to recreate them.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Construct Pipeline([(name, transformer), ..., (name, estimator)]) to chain transformations with a final estimator. Pipeline.fit fits the transformations and final estimator on training data, while predict applies the fitted transformations before prediction. ColumnTransformer applies declared transformers to selected columns, so categorical and numerical columns can use different operations within the same fitted workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Reuse that fitted pipeline for validation and bounded inference rather than fitting a new preprocessing state. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Imagine distance uses the declared numerical transformer while zone uses the fitted category encoder. ColumnTransformer assigns those operations to their named columns. Pipeline chains the resulting transformation with the final estimator. Fit that workflow on training data, then predict validation through the same fitted object. A fixture should check the expected transformed representation and final output for a valid input, and the supplied boundary and failure cases. If an engineer manually prepares validation with a new encoder, it no longer follows this workflow even if the estimator object is unchanged. Trace one row from selected columns through transformations to the estimator so the distinction between fitting the workflow and applying it is visible.

Trace a complete prediction call rather than testing transformations and estimation as unrelated pieces. The incoming raw columns are selected, their fitted operations are applied and the resulting representation reaches the final estimator. Intermediate pipeline steps must support fitting and transformation; the final step is the estimator. A manually prepared validation array can accidentally skip a step or use a newly learned category order, which is why the fixture should exercise the fitted workflow's own prediction path. Preserve column assignment and fitted state together. Successful estimation of an already transformed array is not evidence that the raw-input pipeline handles the declared contract correctly.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A pipeline is not a reason to refit for every cohort. Its predict path applies fitted transformations; changing preprocessing state changes the representation presented to the final estimator.

context.concept_name: Detect target or preprocessing leakage across training and prediction boundaries

coverage.learning_objective: Find and repair one evaluation-information leak without changing the evaluation boundary.

required_facts.statement: Leakage uses information not available at prediction time when building a model and can make held-out performance estimates overly optimistic.
Audit which rows and fields reach fit operations and each prediction, then remove held-out or future information from those operations.
Separate training and evaluation before fitting preprocessing, and call transform rather than fit or fit_transform on held-out inputs.
Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Prevent Prediction-Time Leakage
teaching_blocks.content: A validation result looks unusually strong, but an order's eventual arrival has reached the features. The question is not just whether the evaluation rows were held out. Audit what information reached fitting and what was available for each prediction.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Leakage uses information not available at prediction time when building a model and can make held-out performance estimates overly optimistic. Audit which rows and fields reach fit operations and each prediction, then remove held-out or future information from those operations. Separate training and evaluation before fitting preprocessing, and call transform rather than fit or fit_transform on held-out inputs.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For predictions made at acceptance, a field populated only after arrival is unavailable at the required boundary. Remove it from the prediction input rather than describing the strong held-out result as reliable evidence for this task. Also trace the preprocessing fit: if it saw both training and validation rows, separating the estimator's fit alone did not keep held-out information out of the fitted system. Split before fitting preprocessing and apply transform to held-out inputs. In the bounded fixture, retain explicit checks that no future field enters the prediction and that the fit receives only the designated training rows. The audit is about information flow, not merely whether files have different names.

Distinguish the prediction-time audit from the held-out-fit audit. The former asks whether each input field could have been known at the declared decision time. The latter asks whether any fitted choice used held-out observations. Removing the eventual-arrival feature addresses the first issue but does not repair a scaler already fitted on validation; splitting before fit addresses the second but does not make a future field available at acceptance. Test both information paths in the bounded fixture. The corrected workflow should produce held-out predictions from training-fitted state and decision-available inputs, not merely show a lower score after deleting a suspicious column.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A held-out label file does not guarantee leakage-free evaluation. Future fields and held-out rows reaching preprocessing fits can both violate the intended boundary.

context.concept_name: Derive task-relevant features from prediction-time information

coverage.learning_objective: Compute a prediction-time feature using only records available at that time.

required_facts.statement: A feature for a prediction must be derived only from information available when that prediction is made.
A list comprehension of the form [row for row in records if row["available_at"] <= prediction_time] selects the records available at the declared boundary.
A changing lookup table can yield different training and serving values, so use values from the relevant recorded boundary rather than assuming the latest table is historical.

teaching_blocks.title: Prevent Prediction-Time Leakage
teaching_blocks.content: You are constructing a feature from an order's earlier records. Some records were added after the prediction was made, and a lookup table has changed since then. Build the feature from the recorded availability boundary rather than today's complete view.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A feature for a prediction must be derived only from information available when that prediction is made. A list comprehension of the form [row for row in records if row["available_at"] <= prediction_time] selects the records available at the declared boundary. A changing lookup table can yield different training and serving values, so use values from the relevant recorded boundary rather than assuming the latest table is historical.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Test the feature on the original records and on records augmented with later unavailable observations, asserting that the earlier feature is unchanged. Apply the declared arithmetic feature to the time-filtered records only; for a sum, initialize total = 0 and accumulate total += record["value"] over the accepted list.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose an order has available records with values 2 and 3 at the decision time, plus a later record with value 7. For the declared sum feature, filter by available_at first, initialize the total to zero, and accumulate only the accepted values. The earlier feature is 5, not 12. Add the later record to the test input and assert that the earlier feature remains 5. If the feature also uses a changing lookup value, retrieve the value appropriate to the recorded boundary instead of treating the current lookup as historical. This test checks the feature computation's response to later information; it does not require later records to be deleted from the source system.

Preserve the calculation's order in the code and the test: inspect availability, decide membership, then update the accumulator. Summing every record and later removing a timestamp field would not remove the later record's contribution. Adding the value 7 is a useful invariance test because the earlier prediction boundary has not changed. The historical lookup check is the corresponding question for changing reference state. Both mechanisms enforce the same declared availability boundary, but they concern different inputs to the feature. Retain a boundary fixture for a record at the exact permitted time under the supplied predicate instead of assuming whether equality is included.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A timestamp in the source is not enough if the calculation ignores it. The availability filter must precede the arithmetic, and a latest lookup value is not automatically the value available at an earlier prediction.

media.group_title: Keep feature inputs inside the prediction boundary

segments.label: Use known earlier values to predict the next time step
segments.summary: To predict sales at time t+1 while currently at time t, construct features from values already known, such as those at t and t−1. These earlier-value inputs are called lag features. For a prediction of sales at time t, the corresponding inputs instead start at t−1 and t−2. The available history shifts with each prediction boundary. Using future information would leak information into an earlier prediction.

coverage.learning_objective: Enforce an existing permitted-field and credential-exposure policy in diagnostic records.

required_facts.statement: Data access is governed by authenticated identities and authorization, not merely by possession of a dataset or log file.
Implement the supplied permitted-field policy with dictionary membership checks and create a record containing only the permitted values.
Credentials written into an image or its metadata can be exposed; remove literal credentials from the data/log sample rather than treating them as ordinary diagnostic values.
Keep the credential value in the authorized runtime secret mechanism rather than copying it into a generated record.

teaching_blocks.title: Protect Sensitive ML Assets
teaching_blocks.content: An inspection record contains useful diagnostics and a credential. The dataset or log being readable does not grant permission to redistribute every field. Apply the existing identity and permitted-field policy before creating a new record.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Data access is governed by authenticated identities and authorization, not merely by possession of a dataset or log file. Implement the supplied permitted-field policy with dictionary membership checks and create a record containing only the permitted values. Credentials written into an image or its metadata can be exposed; remove literal credentials from the data/log sample rather than treating them as ordinary diagnostic values.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the credential value in the authorized runtime secret mechanism rather than copying it into a generated record.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied policy permits run_id and row_count, but not token or raw customer values. Construct a dictionary containing the permitted fields using membership checks; the new record should contain the run identifier and count without the credential. Keep the credential in the authorized runtime secret mechanism, not in an image, metadata or diagnostic record. Test a sample containing both permitted and forbidden keys and inspect the resulting record rather than assuming a field was removed. This is implementation of an existing policy, not permission to invent new readers or expand the permitted field list. A useful error report can identify the handling problem without reproducing the literal credential.

Build a new permitted-field dictionary rather than copying the whole input and hoping no forbidden field remains. The membership rule should use the existing allowed-field collection; adding a field because it appears diagnostically useful would change policy. Inspect both the returned dictionary and the captured output. A removed token field in the returned record does not establish non-disclosure if the input was printed beforehand. Runtime credential delivery and diagnostic-field selection address related but distinct handling paths. Keep the credential reference usable by the permitted runtime while keeping its literal value absent from generated data, metadata, images and logs.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Possession of a file is not authorization to expose its contents. Moving a literal credential from a data sample into image metadata or a generated diagnostic record does not remove the exposure risk.
